One way to summarize the comparison of two survival curves is to compute the hazard ratio (HR). There are (at least) two methods to compute this value.

  • Logrank method. As part of the Kaplan-Meier calculations, compute the number of observed events (deaths, usually) in each group ($Oa$, and $Ob$), and the number of expected events assuming a null hypothesis of no difference in survival ($Ea$ and $Eb$). The hazard ratio then is: $$ HR= \\frac{(Oa/Ea)}{(Ob/Eb)} $$
  • Mantel-Haenszel method. First compute V, which is the sum of the hypergeometric variances at each time point. Then compute the hazard ratio as: $$ HR= \\exp\\left(\\frac{(Oa-Ea)}{V}\\right) $$ I got both these equations from chapter 3 of Machin, Cheung and Parmar, Is a "split plot" ANOVA with two factors identical to two-way ANOVA with repeated measures in one factor? if not, what is the distinction?

data.content:
**Answer:**

The main advantage is **greater statistical power**. Harvey Motulsky's most-viewed post (post Id 109, *"Power of Holm's multiple comparison testing compared to others"*, 3,980 views — his highest ViewCount among 137 posts, user Id 25 in `codebase_community`) states that Holm's test "has lots of power" and that its advantage over competing multiple-comparison procedures "is that it has more power." This matches the external evidence: the Holm–Bonferroni method "offers a simple test uniformly more powerful than the Bonferroni correction" (ctx://team/engineering/hydra/kilt/10726541/0000, v1), and "uniformly delivers more power than the simple Bonferroni correction, by testing only the lowest p-value against the strictest criterion, and the higher p-values against progressively less strict criteria" (ctx://team/engineering/hydra/kilt/9444220/0008, v1), while still controlling the family-wise error rate.

In short: Holm–Bonferroni is always at least as powerful as (and typically more powerful than) the simple Bonferroni correction — it is less conservative without losing family-wise error control.

*Minor caveat:* the post's body frames the power advantage explicitly against Tukey/Dunnett (which can compute confidence intervals, unlike the stepwise Holm method); the "more powerful than Bonferroni" framing is supported by the retrieved Wikipedia passages cited above.

final_answer:
**Answer:**

The main advantage is **greater statistical power**. Harvey Motulsky's most-viewed post (post Id 109, *"Power of Holm's multiple comparison testing compared to others"*, 3,980 views — his highest ViewCount among 137 posts, user Id 25 in `codebase_community`) states that Holm's test "has lots of power" and that its advantage over competing multiple-comparison procedures "is that it has more power." This matches the external evidence: the Holm–Bonferroni method "offers a simple test uniformly more powerful than the Bonferroni correction" (ctx://team/engineering/hydra/kilt/10726541/0000, v1), and "uniformly delivers more power than the simple Bonferroni correction, by testing only the lowest p-value against the strictest criterion, and the higher p-values against progressively less strict criteria" (ctx://team/engineering/hydra/kilt/9444220/0008, v1), while still controlling the family-wise error rate.

In short: Holm–Bonferroni is always at least as powerful as (and typically more powerful than) the simple Bonferroni correction — it is less conservative without losing family-wise error control.

*Minor caveat:* the post's body frames the power advantage explicitly against Tukey/Dunnett (which can compute confidence intervals, unlike the stepwise Holm method); the "more powerful than Bonferroni" framing is supported by the retrieved Wikipedia passages cited above.
